title: Concurrency in Python: code drills
seriesTitle: Python: threading, the GIL and asyncio
seriesDescription: Threads, locks, the GIL, concurrent.futures, asyncio, queues and classic drills. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Write-the-code drills: producer-consumer with queue.Queue and asyncio.Queue, Condition-based buffer, thread-safe LRU cache, token-bucket rate limiter, odd/even printing and print-in-order.
source: Python docs: queue, threading, collections, asyncio; Real Python; GeeksforGeeks; LeetCode concurrency problems (print in order, odd/even printing)

questions.prompt: A producer calls `q.put(i, timeout=0.1)` for `i = 1..10` on a `queue.Queue(maxsize=3)` with no consumer running, ignoring `queue.Full` errors. How many `put` calls complete without raising?
questions.explanation: The queue holds 3 items, so exactly 3 puts succeed and the other 7 time out and raise `queue.Full` (verified by running it). That blocking is the back-pressure that makes bounded queues safe.

questions.prompt: Using `queue.Queue(maxsize=10)` named `q`, write a Python producer function that puts the numbers 0..99 followed by `None`, and a consumer function that gets items until `None`, calling `q.task_done()` for every item it took.
questions.explanation: `queue.Queue` is thread-safe with its own locks; `put` blocks when full. `q.join()` then waits until `task_done` has been called for every item. Run each function in a `threading.Thread`.

questions.prompt: With `asyncio.Queue(maxsize=10)` named `q`, write `async def producer()` that awaits putting 0..99, and `async def consumer()` that loops forever awaiting `q.get()` and calling `q.task_done()`. Then write `main()` code that runs both, waits for the queue to drain with `q.join()` and cancels the consumer.

checks.label: consumer awaits q.get and calls task_done

questions.model:
async def producer():
    for i in range(100): await q.put(i)

async def consumer():
    while True:
        item = await q.get(); print(item); q.task_done()

async def main():
    c = asyncio.create_task(consumer())
    await producer()
    await q.join()
    c.cancel()
questions.explanation: Forgetting the `await` on `put/get` is the usual mistake: you get a never-awaited coroutine. The queue is not thread-safe; use it from one event loop.

questions.prompt: In a bounded buffer built on `threading.Condition`, why should a consumer write `"while not self.items: self.cond.wait()"` rather than `"if not self.items: self.cond.wait()"`?

options.text: The state may change before the woken thread runs, so it has to re-test the predicate.
options.why: Correct: a woken thread must re-test, because the state can change before it re-acquires the lock, and wake-ups can be spurious.

options.text: `wait()` raises `RuntimeError` unless it is called from inside a loop body in the same method, always.
options.why: Nothing in the module requires a loop around `wait()`.

options.text: The loop makes the condition fair, so that waiting threads are woken strictly in arrival order.
options.why: Looping has no influence on fairness; it only re-tests the predicate.

options.text: `notify()` will not wake any thread unless the guard in front of `wait()` is written as a loop.
options.why: `notify()` wakes a waiter regardless of how the guard is written.

questions.explanation: `Condition.wait_for(predicate)` packages the loop for you. Always re-check the predicate after any wake-up.

questions.prompt: One producer feeds a shared `queue.Queue` that 4 consumer threads read, and each consumer exits when it gets a `None` sentinel. How many `None` sentinels must the producer put after the last real item so that every consumer terminates?
questions.explanation: A consumer that takes a sentinel exits and never takes another, so each consumer needs its own: 4. (Re-queueing one sentinel before exiting is the alternative.)

questions.prompt: Write a Python class `LRU` with `__init__(self, cap)`, `get(key)` returning `None` on a miss, and `put(key, value)`, using an `OrderedDict` and a `threading.Lock`. A hit and a put both mark the key most recent, and the oldest key is evicted when size exceeds `cap`.
questions.explanation: Verified: the order after `put a, put b, get a, put c` is `[a, c]`. `popitem(last=False)` pops the oldest. `functools.lru_cache` is thread-safe for its own bookkeeping but cannot be inspected like this.

questions.prompt: Complete the recipe for a Python LRU cache built on `collections.OrderedDict`.
questions.text: Mark a key as most recently used with {1}(key), evict the oldest entry with popitem(last={2}), and guard both operations with a Lock used in a {3} statement.
questions.explanation: `popitem(last=True)` would pop the newest entry, which is a stack, not an LRU. `functools.lru_cache` gives the same policy for pure functions out of the box.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: In an `OrderedDict`-based LRU cache, `get()` must take the same lock as `put()`.
questions.reason: A cache hit calls `move_to_end`, which changes the recency order and therefore mutates the shared structure.

whys.a: Correct: a hit is a write to the order, so reads cannot run unguarded or under a shared read lock.
whys.b: R is the direct cause of A, so calling it merely true understates the link.
whys.c: R is true, so option c (R false) is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so option d (A false) is wrong.

questions.explanation: This is why a read-write lock gives no gain for an LRU cache: every hit changes recency.

questions.prompt: Write a thread-safe Python class `TokenBucket(cap, rate)` where tokens start full and refill at `rate` tokens per second up to `cap`. `allow()` refills lazily from the elapsed time (`time.monotonic`), consumes one token if at least one is available and returns `True`, otherwise `False`.
questions.explanation: Verified: a bucket of 3 answers `[True, True, True, False, False]` for five instant calls. The lock matters because refill and consume are one read-modify-write.

questions.prompt: Two threads print 1..n alternately, odd numbers first. Semaphores `sem_odd = Semaphore(1)` and `sem_even = Semaphore(0)` already exist. Write `odd(n)` and `even(n)` so the output is `1 2 3 ... n` in order.
questions.explanation: Verified for `n = 9` with two threads. Each semaphore acts as a baton. A `threading.Condition` with a shared turn variable and `wait_for` is the alternative.

questions.prompt: Three threads run `first()`, `second()` and `third()` in an arbitrary start order, but the output must always be first, second, third. Using two `threading.Event` objects `e1` and `e2`, write the three functions (each prints its own name).
questions.explanation: Each `Event` is a one-shot gate: later steps wait for the earlier signal. Verified with threads started in the order third, first, second. Two semaphores or a `Condition` with a turn variable also work.
questions.starter:
import threading
e1, e2 = threading.Event(), threading.Event()

questions.prompt: Write a Python class `Buffer(cap)` holding a `collections.deque` and one `threading.Condition`. `put(x)` must wait while the buffer is full and `take()` must wait while it is `empty;` both wake the other side with `notify_all`.

checks.label: waits on a predicate (loop or wait_for)

questions.model:
import threading
from collections import deque

class Buffer:
    def __init__(self, cap):
        self.q, self.cap = deque(), cap
        self.cond = threading.Condition()

    def put(self, x):
        with self.cond:
            self.cond.wait_for(lambda: len(self.q) < self.cap)
            self.q.append(x)
            self.cond.notify_all()

    def take(self):
        with self.cond:
            self.cond.wait_for(lambda: self.q)
            v = self.q.popleft()
            self.cond.notify_all()
            return v
questions.explanation: Verified with one producer and one consumer. `wait_for` re-tests the predicate after every wake-up, replacing the hand-written while loop; `notify_all` is safer than `notify` because producers and consumers share one wait set. `queue.Queue` already does all of this.

questions.prompt: An LRU cache with capacity 3 receives `put(1)`, `put(2)`, `put(3)`, `get(1)`, `put(4)`, `put(5)`. What is the sum of the keys still cached?
questions.explanation: `get(1)` makes the order 2, 3, 1; `put(4)` evicts 2; `put(5)` evicts 3, leaving 1, 4 and 5, so the sum is 10 (verified with an `OrderedDict`).

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: `threading.Condition.wait()` can be called by a thread that has not acquired the condition lock.
questions.reason: `wait()` releases the underlying lock while the thread sleeps and re-acquires it before returning.

whys.a: A is false, so option a (A true) is wrong.
whys.b: A is false, so option b (both true) is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so option c (R false) is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: calling wait() without holding the lock raises RuntimeError ("cannot wait on un-acquired lock", verified), while R correctly describes what wait() does with the lock.

questions.explanation: Hold the condition (`with cond:`) around every wait and notify. The release-and-reacquire in `wait()` is what lets other threads change the state you are waiting for.
